evidence.claim: Tannery roads and mountain resorts behind a Catskill clove drive
evidence.quote: NY 214 was part of a tannery road constructed by Colonel William Edwards of Hunter in the late 1840s, opening by 1849. The road was upgraded in 1873 to the Stoney Clove Turnpike, which serviced hotels and resorts in the Catskills.

evidence.claim: Mountain Cloves links 41 miles of roads in the northern high peaks of the Catskills.
evidence.quote: Length: 41 miles Region: Catskill Mountains Connects: Various Scenic Roads in the Town of Hunter

evidence.claim: Route 23A passes Hunter Mountain before descending through Kaaterskill Clove toward the Hudson Valley.
evidence.quote: The route passes several of the Catskill High Peaks, including Hunter Mountain, before dropping into the Hudson Valley via Kaaterskill Clove

evidence.claim: New York State approved the branched scenic byway in 2013.
evidence.quote: in 2013, the state of New York approved a bill creating the Mountain Cloves Scenic Byway, which is a 41-mile (66 km) byway with multiple branches serving the Catskill Mountains.

evidence.claim: The state transportation department identifies scenic, recreational, historic and natural themes, linking its mountain and valley views with the Hudson River School painters.
evidence.quote: This same Catskill aura influenced the Hudson River School of landscape painters of the mid-19th Century American art movement.

evidence.claim: The state transportation department identifies scenic, recreational, historic and natural themes
evidence.quote: Themes: Scenic, Recreational, Historic, Natural

evidence.claim: One branch began with hemlock bark: Colonel William Edwards built the predecessor of Route 214 to supply his Hunter tannery.
evidence.quote: This road was constructed along the clove that marks eastern flank of Hunter Mountain and western of Plateau Mountain in the Catskills so that Edwards to get hemlock tree bark to the tannery from the mountains.

evidence.claim: Open by 1849, it became the Stoney Clove Turnpike in 1873, serving hotels and resorts.
evidence.quote: NY 214 was part of a tannery road constructed by Colonel William Edwards of Hunter in the late 1840s, opening by 1849. The road was upgraded in 1873 to the Stoney Clove Turnpike, which serviced hotels and resorts in the Catskills.

evidence.claim: The numbered highway came in 1930; between 1946 and 1956, Lanesville residents fought to rebuild an unsafe school-bus route.
evidence.quote: In 1930, the route was designated as NY 214, but the part in Greene County was not state-maintained, instead by the county. From 1946 to 1956, the residents of the hamlet of Lanesville spent time fighting for NY 214 to be reconstructed due to being an unsafe dirt road for their children to attend school using their bus.

evidence.claim: For the eastward drive, Route 23A becomes Hunter village’s main street, then meets Route 214 at Stony Clove Notch.
evidence.quote: The highway continues east into Hunter, one of only a handful of communities along NY 23A, becoming the village's main street.

evidence.claim: Past the junction, Plateau, Sugarloaf, Twin and Indian Head mountains rise south of the road before Tannersville.
evidence.quote: Past Plateau Mountain, the remainder of the range—Sugarloaf, Twin and Indian Head mountains—rise to the south as the road continues east.

evidence.claim: Continue through Haines Falls and descend into Kaaterskill Clove; the road levels just west of Palenville.
evidence.quote: The road levels off just west of Palenville, where it crosses the Long Path hiking trail and leaves the Catskill Park.

evidence.claim: then meets Route 214 at Stony Clove Notch.
evidence.quote: NY 23A connects to NY 214 at the north end of Stony Clove Notch

evidence.claim: Continue through Haines Falls and descend into Kaaterskill Clove
evidence.quote: The distinctive ridgeline of Kaaterskill High Peak and its shorter neighbor, Round Top Mountain, appear just east of the hamlet along with the dramatic drop into Kaaterskill Clove

evidence.claim: Pastel buildings and cartoon-like shutter paintings give Tannersville’s downtown its unusual palette.
evidence.quote: The Paint Project involves painting downtown buildings in multicolored pastels, often with cartoon-like pictures on the shutters.

evidence.claim: The Hunter Foundation’s Paint Program grew from local artist Elena Patterson’s vision, supported by Mayor Glenn Weyant, sponsors and residents.
evidence.quote: The Hunter Foundation has implemented the town-wide "Paint Program" — the vision of Elena Patterson, a local artist — with the help and support of Glenn Weyant who was the mayor at the time, corporate sponsors, and local residents.

evidence.claim: The village began with lumber mills and tanneries; after tanning collapsed in the mid-19th century, summer resorts gradually took its place.
evidence.quote:
The village was founded around lumber mills and tanneries. It was incorporated in 1895.
Tannersville's tanning business collapsed in the mid-19th century. It was gradually replaced by the summer resort trade

evidence.claim: Rail service arrived in 1882, but the automobile later loosened visitors’ ties to a single summer destination.
evidence.quote: which reached its peak in 1882 when the railroad came to Tannersville. However, the rise of the automobile in the early 20th century led to a steady economic decline, as travelers were no longer rooted to one spot for an entire summer.

evidence.claim: Route 23A is the village’s Main Street.
evidence.quote: NY 23A is Tannersville's Main Street

evidence.claim: Kaaterskill Falls drops in two stages between Haines Falls and Palenville.
evidence.quote: Kaaterskill Falls is a two-stage waterfall on Spruce Creek in the eastern Catskill Mountains of New York, between the hamlets of Haines Falls and Palenville in Greene County.

evidence.claim: The shelf between the cascades marks a boundary between Devonian rock formations, with a large pool between the falls.
evidence.quote: The shelf dividing the two falls (and creating the large pool between them) is the break between the Manorkill Sandstone formed in the Middle Devonian period and the Oneonta-Genesee sandstone-shale mixture of the late Devonian period.

evidence.claim: Thomas Cole first visited in 1825, and the falls became a subject for Hudson River School painters.
evidence.quote: Beginning with Thomas Cole's first visit during 1825, they became a subject for painters of the Hudson River School

evidence.claim: Asher Durand’s Kindred Spirits combines the falls and neighboring clove features into an imagined view.
evidence.quote: a landscape that synthesized the falls and parts of the surrounding clove, including Haines Falls, into a landscape that, while visually striking, is really an imagined view of the falls.

evidence.claim: The landscape in that painting is a composition, rather than a single viewpoint to seek out.
evidence.quote: is really an imagined view of the falls.

evidence.claim: Kaaterskill Creek runs through Palenville at the foot of the clove.
evidence.quote: It lies at the foot of Kaaterskill Clove, at the base of the Catskill Mountains. Kaaterskill Creek, exiting the Clove, runs through the town

evidence.claim: The hamlet takes its name from the Palen family, whose Catskill tanneries depended on hemlock bark.
evidence.quote: Palenville takes its name from the Palen family, who built and operated tanneries throughout the Catskills starting in the 1820s. The tannery era was short. When the local supply of hemlock bark was exhausted, the tannery closed

evidence.claim: When the local bark supply ran out, the tannery closed.
evidence.quote: When the local supply of hemlock bark was exhausted, the tannery closed

evidence.claim: Tourism followed, with boardinghouses and a claim to be the home of the fictional Rip Van Winkle.
evidence.quote: Palenville reinvented itself as a tourist town, building several boardinghouses and proclaiming itself the home of the fictional character Rip van Winkle.

evidence.claim: Thomas Cole and Frederic Church stayed and worked here during the Hudson River School’s height.
evidence.quote: Thomas Cole, Frederic Church, and other notable painters stayed and worked in Palenville during the height of the movement.

evidence.claim: Mountain Cloves links 41 miles of roads in the northern high peaks of the Catskills.
evidence.quote: within the northern high peaks of the Catskill Mountains.

evidence.claim: In 1994, the town of Hunter, the Catskill Center for Conservation and Development and Greene County planners nominated roads through Stony, Kaaterskill and Platte cloves for the state scenic-roads program.
evidence.quote: In March 1994, the town of Hunter, the Catskill Center for Conservation and Development and the Greene County Planning Department nominated NY 214 along with the Kaaterskill Clove portion of NYS 23A and the clove portion of Platte Clove Rd. to the New York State Scenic Roads Program.

evidence.claim: A separate branch, Route 214, narrows the landscape to Stony Clove Notch between Hunter and Plateau mountains.
evidence.quote: At this junction, NY 214 turns northward between Plateau and Hunter mountains, becoming a two-lane woods road.

evidence.claim: The village sits just west of the high ground dividing drainage toward the Schoharie from water descending east through Kaaterskill Clove to the Hudson Valley.
evidence.quote: just west of the height of land on New York State Route 23A: Sawmill Creek flows southwest through the center of the village into Gooseberry Creek and thence into Schoharie Creek, a north-flowing tributary of the Mohawk River, while just 2 miles (3 km) to the east, at Haines Falls, Kaaterskill Creek drops east into Kaaterskill Clove and thence into the Hudson River valley.

evidence.claim: Asher Durand’s Kindred Spirits combines the falls and neighboring clove features into an imagined view.
evidence.quote: One of the best-known depictions of the falls is Asher Durand's Kindred Spirits (1849), a stylized rendition.

evidence.claim: Cole’s paintings helped attract affluent visitors to the Catskill Mountain House and neighboring hotels; the waterfall also inspired William Cullen Bryant’s poem Catterskill Falls.
evidence.quote: Their work attracted affluent visitors to the Catskill Mountain House and the other hotels established near it later.

evidence.claim: the waterfall also inspired William Cullen Bryant’s poem Catterskill Falls.
evidence.quote: The Falls also inspired "Catterskill Falls", a poem by William Cullen Bryant.

evidence.claim: At the turn of the century, nearly two dozen boardinghouses and many hotels served vacationers here.
evidence.quote: hosting nearly two dozen small and medium-sized boarding houses and many hotels at the turn of the century.
